entries.q: What should we know about your life story?
entries.a: I was born in Ranchi, and we moved to the UAE when I was five, so I actually grew up in Abu Dhabi and did all my schooling there — Asian International School in Ruwais, right through twelfth. Two things stuck from early on: football, which I still play, and computers. I came back to India for my B.Tech at SRM in Chennai, and that's where AI really got me — I ended up publishing a paper comparing five deep learning architectures for spotting lung cancer in CT scans. Since then it's been an internship at ADNOC Refining in Abu Dhabi, a stint at Innov8 in Dubai owning payroll and access control, and now I'm in Bangalore building security tooling for AI agents.

entries.q: What's your #1 superpower?
entries.a: I pick things up fast. Hand me something I've never touched and I'll be useful with it in about a day — that's how I went from not knowing NestJS to owning a payroll module and a 299-permission access layer, and from not knowing LangGraph to shipping two agents, inside roughly a year. The part that makes it work is that I'm comfortable being the person in the room who doesn't know yet, so I ask early instead of quietly flailing.

entries.q: What are the top 3 areas you'd like to grow in?
entries.a: Leadership, first. I want to run teams, not just ship my piece — own the operational side and actually help scale something. Second, public speaking. I'm fine one-to-one or with another engineer, but my presence drops in front of a big or cross-functional room, and I'm working on that deliberately. Third, going deeper technically rather than wider — I've covered a lot of ground quickly and I want more depth in the systems I keep reaching for.

entries.q: What are your main strengths?
entries.a: Four, honestly. I learn new tools fast — I've picked up LangGraph, pgvector, MCP and Cloudflare Workers inside real projects rather than tutorials. I'm good with deadlines; I deliver when I said I would, and this bot going out in a day is the most recent proof. I work well in a team and I think I lift the people around me — I end up being the one who unblocks others. And communication: I can explain a technical trade-off to someone who doesn't share my context and have them actually walk away with it.

entries.q: What's your biggest weakness?
entries.a: Saying no is the big one — I've overcommitted because I wanted to be useful. Now I make myself check what's actually on my plate before I answer. I also used to refuse to ask for help, which was just slow; I've got a rule now that if I'm stuck for forty-five minutes I go and ask. And I'm soft-spoken, so I used to dodge giving direct criticism, which isn't fair on the other person. I handle that by talking about the behaviour rather than them, and framing it as a problem we're solving together.

entries.q: What misconception do your coworkers have about you?
entries.a: That I'm unapproachable. I go quite deep into whatever I'm working on, and apparently from the outside that reads as "don't bother him". It's not that at all — once people have worked with me for a week they find I'm pretty open and I like the collaborative part. The other version of it is people assuming I have no life outside work because I care a lot about getting the quality right. I just hold a high bar during work hours; outside them I'm playing football.

entries.q: How do you push your boundaries and limits?
entries.a: I strategize rather than just grind. Mostly it comes down to deliberately choosing the uncomfortable option: I take on the thing I don't know how to finish yet, and I do it in small repeatable steps so the fear wears off instead of building up. I try to treat mistakes as data rather than proof I can't do it. And I only push where it serves a real goal — I'm not chasing stress for its own sake. The main thing I've learned is to act before I feel ready, because the comfort never arrives first.

entries.q: What project are you most proud of?
entries.a: MCP-Hardener, easily. It's a seven-package TypeScript monorepo that turns an OpenAPI spec into a hardened MCP server for AI agents — read-only by default, writes held behind a single-use approval bound to a hash of the exact arguments, tenant IDs stripped from anything the agent can see. There's a gateway that enforces the same rules on third-party servers, and a scanner that fails the build on high-severity findings. About 350 tests. It's live at hardened-mcp.mcphardener.workers.dev.

entries.q: Tell me about a time you failed.
entries.a: On the payroll work I shipped the month-lock on creating records but not on editing them, so a processed payroll month was closed to new entries and still quietly editable. The frozen payslips meant no money was wrong, but the live records and the snapshot could drift — exactly the class of bug I'd said I was there to prevent. I found it by probing a processed run rather than by reading the code, and that's the real lesson: I assume a guard I haven't attacked isn't a guard yet.

entries.q: How do you handle disagreement?
entries.a: I try to turn it into a question about consequences rather than taste. On the HR product I wanted platform-admin accounts creatable only by hand, against the database — no endpoint, no seeder — and that's less convenient, so it needed defending. The argument that worked wasn't "it's safer", it was "any code path in the running app that can mint a super admin is an escalation path for anyone who reaches it". When someone pushes back and they're right, I'd rather change my mind fast and say so.

entries.q: How do you handle criticism of your work?
entries.a: I try to treat it as data rather than a verdict — if someone's right, changing my mind quickly is cheaper than defending a position I've stopped believing. Code review is the easy version and I want more of it; I've been building mostly alone, and a team that catches me is one of the things I'm looking for. Giving criticism was the harder direction for me — I used to avoid it, which didn't help anyone, so now I talk about the behaviour rather than the person.

entries.a: Connecting an agent to a tool server is a one-liner, and what it gets back is usually completely unguarded — delete is as reachable as read, and a tool's description is read by the model as instructions. That gap is the thing I keep coming back to, and it's why I built MCP-Hardener. It's a security problem and a plumbing problem at the same time, which suits me.

entries.q: Why are you the best person for this role?

I also bring the boring strengths: a 299-permission layer across 380-plus endpoints, a migration safe to re-run before a 14,000-user cutover, 350-plus tests on my own project with nobody making me. entries.q: Why did you choose computer science?

entries.q: How do you work under pressure and tight deadlines?
entries.a: Deadlines are honestly where I'm at my best — I'd rather have a date than an open-ended brief. This bot is the recent example: a day to build it, including two APIs I'd never touched. The way I handle it is to get something working end to end badly first, then make it good, so there's always something shippable. What I've learned not to do is quietly absorb more scope while the date stays fixed.

entries.q: How do you prioritise when everything is urgent?
entries.a: I look at what actually breaks if it slips, and what blocks someone else — the thing another person is waiting on goes first, because my delay becomes their delay. Then I'm honest about bandwidth instead of agreeing to everything. That's something I've had to learn: I used to say yes reflexively and overcommit, so now I check what's already on the list before answering.

entries.q: Do you prefer working alone or on a team?
entries.a: A team, and I think I'm good in one — I tend to end up as the person who unblocks other people, so the team's output goes up more than mine does. I can go heads-down when something needs deep focus, and most of my own projects were built that way. But doing it entirely alone is what I'm trying to get away from; what I want next is a team with a higher bar than mine.

entries.q: Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly.
entries.a: This bot, honestly. I had a day, and I'd never used the Gemini Live API or Cloudflare Workers — so I built the simplest thing that could speak, then layered on the WebSocket proxy, the barge-in and the fallbacks. Before that it was LangGraph for KubeMedic and the MCP spec for MCP-Hardener, both picked up inside a real project rather than a tutorial. Having something that has to work by a date is what makes it stick for me.

entries.q: How do you deal with ambiguity or unclear requirements?
entries.a: I ask the question that changes the answer, and I don't ask the rest. Usually that's about consequences — what happens if this runs twice, who's allowed to call this, what the number means when the data is missing. Where I can't get an answer I pick the safer reading, build it, and say out loud what I assumed so it's easy to correct. Waiting for perfect clarity just moves the risk later.

entries.q: What motivates you?
entries.a: Building something that solves a real problem for someone, and that holds up. The unglamorous half is what I actually enjoy — the migration you can safely run twice, the permission check nobody can skip. The long-term version is that I want to build a self-sufficient business that solves a real problem in the world, so working on things that matter to the people using them is the practice for that.

entries.q: What would your last manager say about you?
entries.a: That I deliver when I said I would, and that I own the thing rather than the ticket — at Innov8 I had payroll, notifications and access control end to end and nobody had to chase me. I think they'd also say I go quiet when I'm deep in something, which reads as unapproachable until you know me. And probably that I'd rather raise the awkward question about permissions early than discover it in production.

entries.q: How would you describe your working style?
entries.a: Deep focus in long blocks, and a bias towards getting something running early so there's a real thing to argue about. I write tests as I go — 350-plus on my own project — because it's how I know the claim is true. I like owning a whole slice end to end. And I'd rather over-communicate the assumption I made than have someone find it a week later.

entries.q: What's your long-term ambition?
entries.a: Two things. I want to grow into leading teams — broader operational strategy, helping scale a business, not just the code inside it. And the longer-term dream is to build a self-sufficient business that solves a real problem in the world, something that stands on its own rather than a startup for its own sake. The nearer step is deeper ownership and getting properly good in front of a room.

entries.q: Do you have leadership experience?
entries.a: Not formally managing anyone yet, and I'd rather say that straight. What I have is ownership — at Innov8 I ran payroll, notifications and access control end to end, decided how the permission model worked, and defended those calls. Leading teams is exactly where I want to grow next, along with being better in front of larger, cross-functional groups. So it's an honest gap and a deliberate direction, not something I'm claiming.

entries.q: Why do you care so much about security?
entries.a: Because discipline doesn't hold at three in the morning, and systems shouldn't depend on it. Working on payroll made that concrete — people get paid from that code. With agents it's sharper: handing an agent a tool server is a one-liner, and what it gets is usually completely unguarded, where delete is as reachable as read. I'd rather the blast radius be a property of the configuration than of the upstream author's good intentions.

entries.q: How do you think about testing?
entries.a: Tests are how I earn the right to claim something works. MCP-Hardener has 350-plus and nobody was making me write one. The ETL pipeline has twenty-five that run with no database and no API key, so they actually get run. I also trust probing over reading — the payroll month-lock bug I found by attacking a processed run, not by reviewing code.

entries.q: How did you build this voice bot?
entries.a: Three tiers, so it can't dead-end on you. Tier one is the Gemini Live API over a WebSocket — mic in, spoken audio out, with barge-in. If that can't start, tier two uses the browser's own speech recognition and synthesis around a text model. If there's no network, tier three answers from a prepared bank. The key bit is that the browser never holds the API key: a Cloudflare Worker proxies the socket and sends the setup frame itself, so the persona can't be swapped by editing the page's JavaScript.

entries.q: How do you keep up with new technology?
entries.a: By building with it — reading about something doesn't stick for me. MCP is the clearest case: the spec was new, so I went and built a hardening layer for it and found out where it's weak. Otherwise I follow it fairly closely out of genuine interest; upcoming tech is what I read about for fun. But the filter is whether I can make something with it.
